pr_title: Improve code coverage on collections with stream-based flows
pr_body:
- Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/32145 (Improve code coverage on collections with Stream-based flows).

    Collection converters are fully covered (line & branch). There are still some gaps in `IEnumerableDefaultConverter`, `ObjectDefaultConverter`, and `DictionaryDefaultConverter`. I plan to address those in a follow up as apart of https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/32341.

    **Before**
![before](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/9868994/80338348-f638e700-8810-11ea-8ce6-20bb779a65e7.png)

    **After**
![after](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/9868994/80338368-018c1280-8811-11ea-82ab-7ede54f2f942.png)

- Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/34564 (JsonSerializer intermittently writes invalid JSON for dictionaries in .NET 5 preview 2).

    Some of the dictionary converters didn't have logic need to resume when the reader fails to read the entire key.

- Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/35278 (Issue when combining ReferenceHandling.Preserve and DeserializeAsync).

    There were bugs with parsing metadata related to reference handling on deserialization: "id", "ref", "values". The responsible method did not have logic required to resume when `reader.Read()` fails.

- Adds misc branch coverage tests for deserializing collections.

issue_context.title: Improve code coverage on collections with Stream-based flows
issue_context.body:
As part of https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/2259, we deferred adding tests for every collection type due in part to keep the PR smaller (already too large to effectively review).

Specifically every collection type needs to be tests for running out of data on reads (reader.Read() returns false) and for hitting the "flush size" during write.

Whitespace can be added the the buffer to ensure each branch is hit (verified through code coverage).

For reference tests, see System.Text.Json.Serialization.Tests.StreamTests.FlushThresholdTest(), ReadSimpleObjectAsync(), and ReadAsync(). The implementation should create a custom Stream that can detect when ReadAsync()\FlushAsync() are called.

review_comments:
Aside from applying review feedback, changes here are mostly cosmetic to make the code a bit cleaner & easier to read.

I also remove asserts on serialized dictionaries with `ReferenceHandling.Preserve`. Since ~reflection ordering~ the order of elements returned by the enumerator is not guaranteed, the serialized `ref`/`id` metadata values might not match up between multiple serialization operations, which makes the serialized results hard to compare.

> reflection ordering is not guaranteed -- ref/id metadata values might not match up.

Hmm, what does reflection ordering has to do with dictionary KeyValuePairs and metadata? 
Doesn't reflection ordering only affects the order of object's properties?

I meant the order of elements returned by `.GetEnumerator()` for dictionaries, which is the order we serialize & check for metadata. The order is not guaranteed (except for some special types e.g. `OrderedDictionary` & `SortedDictionary`). I hit a few test failures because of this locally, most frequently for `ConcurrentDictionary<,>`.

> which is the order we serialize & check for metadata.

We don't check for metadata on serialization, we append metadata to the resulting JSON objects and collections; metadata properties are never part of the CLR object.
Could it be that the issue that you are facing is caused by a race condition bug in the test?

> > which is the order we serialize & check for metadata.
> 
> We don't check for metadata on serialization

check for **references***

We check if we have seen the instance before in order to assign it metadata, and that is done in the order returned by the enumerator.

The dictionary element that takes an "id" of "1" when we serialize may not be the same one that takes it during the next serialization.

> Could it be that the issue that you are facing is caused by a race condition bug in the test?

I don't believe so.

As we discussed offline, a Dictionary enumeration returns elements in a non-deterministic manner on Serialization time, which will cause that its elements don't get the same id on each call. So condition on line 99 `if(!(DictionaryTypes<TElement>().Contains(type) && options.ReferenceHandling == ReferenceHandling.Preserve))` is correct.

After this PR is merged, I'll open an issue discussing ways we can run the test for the `if(DictionaryTypes<TElement>().Contains(type) && options.ReferenceHandling == ReferenceHandling.Preserve)` case. One way is to override the GetEnumerator method and force a particular order.
Removed the `Metadata` prefix on these values as the names were getting too long to read/understand quickly. I think the intent is clear in the respective call sites.
Before this we were silently failing (i.e. not throwing) when there was invalid JSON as the value of a parameter that wasn't a candidate for deserialization, right? Did you add a test for this?

No -  this code path applies only when `reader.IsFinalBlock` is true, so `reader.TrySkip` was always `true` here. This code path has full test coverage.

It would be good to have tests focused on encountering invalid JSON when deserializing objects (with both parameterless & parameterized ctors) & when deserializing when `options.ReferenceHandling.Preserve` is active, similar to work done in https://github.com/dotnet/corefx/pull/42254 & https://github.com/dotnet/corefx/pull/42066. I logged an issue to track this - https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/35517.

> This code path has full test coverage.

What's the reason for this change, then?

Are you asking why was changed in this PR? I noticed it while skimming through the files for places where we throw when `reader.TokenType != JsonTokenType.PropertyName` (in some cases, `Debug.Assert` is fine). I thought to change it since I have context here.

---
Otherwise,

`TrySkip` is meant for when the reader might not have the data needed for the children to be skipped successfully. We know that's not the case here.

Using `Skip` provides extra validation for this assumption because `InvalidOperationException` is thrown if `IsFinalBlock` is false.

> Using Skip provides extra validation for this assumption because InvalidOperationException is thrown if IsFinalBlock is false.

This seems reasonable to me, and its the answer to what I was trying to ask. Thanks.
What's the reason for this change?

The initial code is incorrect, as the enumerator for these collections can't be cast to `Dictionary<string, TValue>.Enumerator`. We didn't have coverage for this scenario (resuming after fetching more data during async deserialization of immutable dictionaries) prior to this PR. We'd have leaked an `InvalidCastException`.
So this was the only collection we didn't apply the "ShouldFlush" pattern to?
Yup.

Yup.
